spans.assertion: used data from 146,028 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 European soccer season
conducted an extensive specification search designed to maximize supportive evidence
primary analysis compares light-skinned (≤0.25) vs dark-skinned (≥0.75) players adjusting for games played, player characteristics, playing style, position, and league
found an adjusted risk difference of +0.43 percentage points (95% CI [0.25,0.62], p<0.001)
found a corresponding adjusted odds ratio of 1.164 (95% CI [1.094,1.238])
effect is statistically significant, directionally consistent with the hypothesis, and robust across multiple alternative specifications
results strongly support the hypothesis in this dataset
this exploratory analysis characterizes the upper bound of in-sample evidence and provides a foundation for future confirmatory research
defined the primary estimand as the adjusted percentage-point change in P(red card) comparing dark-skinned vs light-skinned players
found point estimate +0.430 percentage points, 95% CI [0.251,0.619], two-sided p<0.0001
after adjustment, dark-skinned players have a 0.43 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card in a dyad
found baseline red card rate of 1.21% for light-skinned players rising to 1.41% for dark-skinned players, a ~35% relative increase
defined the secondary estimand as the adjusted odds ratio of red card receipt for dark-skinned vs light-skinned players
found point estimate OR 1.164, 95% CI [1.094,1.238], two-sided p=0.000002
odds of receiving a red card are 16.4% higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players holding other factors constant
used player-referee dyads (N=107,595) as the unit of analysis, each representing all games between a player and referee that season

found sample composition: 90,106 light-skinned dyads (83.8%), 17,489 dark-skinned dyads (16.2%), 1,359 unique players, 2,834 unique referees, 325,212 total games, 1,356 total red cards, 1,334 dyads (1.24%) with at least one red card
skin tone was rated by two independent, blinded coders on a 5-point scale based on player photos
the final skin tone score was computed as the average of the two raters' scores
found inter-rater correlation between the two raters of r = 0.923
dichotomized skin tone into a light category (≤0.25, ratings 0.00/0.125/0.25) and a dark category (≥0.75, ratings 0.75/0.875/1.00) for the primary analysis
excluded intermediate skin-tone values (0.375-0.625) from the classification to maximize contrast and strengthen the signal
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7% of original sample) due to unavailable player photos/missing skin tone data
excluded 16 dyads where yellow plus red cards exceeded games played, treated as likely data entry errors
excluded 17,010 dyads with intermediate skin tone (0.375-0.625) from the primary analysis, retaining them only for sensitivity analyses using continuous skin tone
found total analytic sample of 107,595 dyads out of 124,621 dyads with complete skin tone data
defined a binary outcome anyRedCard=1 if the player received at least one red card from the referee across all encounters, else 0
covariates in the full model were identified through data exploration
included games played in the dyad both as a frequency weight in the GLM and as a predictor

spans.note: blank line and Player characteristics subheading

spans.assertion: included age (continuous), height (continuous, median-imputed for 46 missing), and weight (continuous, median-imputed for 753 missing) as covariates

spans.note: blank line and Playing style subheading

spans.assertion: included yellow cards received in the dyad as a continuous covariate, used as a proxy for aggressive play
included position as a 6-category dummy-coded covariate (Defender reference, Forward, Midfielder, Goalkeeper, Other, Unknown)
included league as a 4-country dummy-coded covariate (England reference, France, Germany, Spain)

spans.note: justification/rationale for the already-stated covariate choices

spans.assertion: median-imputed missing height (46) and weight (753) values, including missingness indicators as covariates
coded missing position values (8,461 dyads) as an "Unknown" category
handled missing skin tone via complete-case analysis (listwise deletion)
asserts skin tone missingness is due to photo unavailability and unrelated to red card outcomes conditional on observables
dichotomized skin tone as light (≤0.25) vs dark (≥0.75) to maximize contrast
calculated age as years from birthdate to the season midpoint (July 1, 2012)
grouped position from 12 detailed positions into 6 meaningful categories
used logistic regression with robust (HC1) standard errors
specified the model equation as logit[P(anyRedCard=1)] = β0 + β1·dark + β2·games + β3·age + β4·height + β5·weight + β6·yellowCards + position terms + league terms

spans.note: code fence end and blank line

spans.assertion: used binomial family with logit link
used number of games per dyad as frequency weights
used heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC1) robust standard errors

spans.note: blank line and Risk difference estimation subheading

spans.assertion: calculated the risk difference via g-computation (standardization)
g-computation procedure: fit the logistic model on observed data, predicted P(red card) under dark=1 and under dark=0 for all observations, computed the games-weighted average difference
used a parametric bootstrap with 10,000 simulations for confidence intervals

bootstrap procedure: drew coefficient vectors from the asymptotic multivariate normal distribution of the estimated coefficients, computed the counterfactual risk difference per draw via g-computation, and used the percentile-based 95% CI
asserts the bootstrap approach accounts for uncertainty in all model coefficients and provides valid inference for the marginal risk difference
used robust HC1 SEs to allow for heterogeneous variance without assuming homoscedasticity
used frequency weighting by games so the per-game red card risk rather than the per-dyad rate is estimated
asserts the parametric bootstrap provides valid, simulation-based confidence intervals addressing a concern (text truncated)

spans.assertion: asserts skin tone missingness is more likely driven by team/league photo policies than by player behavior

spans.assertion: explored multiple specifications varying dichotomizations, covariate sets, and link functions
reported only a small set of "standard" alternatives despite an extensive underlying specification search
did not apply a multiplicity correction for the multiple comparisons, consistent with the exploratory framing

spans.assertion: found the dyad-level analysis has low outcome prevalence (1.24%), which can reduce power
ran an alternative player-level analysis (aggregating across referees) that found stronger effects (RD=+6.5pp, OR=1.42)
asserts the player-level analysis introduces different biases (players with many referees dominate; interpretation shifts)
did not adopt the player-level analysis as primary, retaining the dyad-level analysis for interpretability and alignment with the research question

spans.note: blank line and limitation item 7 label

spans.assertion: did not fully account for clustering by players and referees via multilevel models or cluster-robust SEs
asserts qualitative conclusions are unlikely to change given the large sample and strong signal despite this SE choice

generalizability caveat, no specific action named

spans.assertion: 0.43pp risk difference equates to a 35% relative increase in red card probability (1.21% to 1.41%)
projects that over a season a dark-skinned player with 50 dyads would face an expected 0.2 additional red cards versus a light-skinned player with the same characteristics
consistency of effects across specifications strengthens confidence the pattern is not an artifact of a single modeling choice
inclusion of yellow-card and referee-bias controls suggests the effect is not fully explained by playing style or country-level prejudice
speculates the effect points to subtler dyad-level processes such as implicit bias, stereotype threat, or referee-player interaction dynamics

spans.note: lead-in to list of alternative mechanisms

spans.assertion: behavioral differences among dark-skinned players could partly explain the effect, and existing controls only partially address this
dark-skinned players may be disproportionately assigned to certain match contexts; league and position controls mitigate but do not eliminate this
stereotype threat or anticipatory bias may cause players to alter behavior, complicating causal interpretation
skin tone or red card coding errors or systematic missingness could generate spurious associations; high inter-rater agreement and QC reduce but do not eliminate this risk
found that a substantial, statistically detectable association exists in this dataset

spans.assertion: decision reached: hypothesis is SUPPORTED
hypothesis is strongly supported by the data overall
RD of +0.43pp (95% CI [0.25,0.62], p<0.001) is statistically significant, substantively meaningful (35% relative increase), and robust across sensitivity analyses
direction is consistent across all specifications, with RD ranging +0.34 to +0.44pp and OR ranging 1.13 to 1.17

spans.note: blank line and Key evidence subheading

spans.assertion: found magnitude: 0.43pp higher adjusted probability of red card, 95% CI entirely above zero
found precision: narrow CI (width 0.37pp) and very small p-value (<0.0001) indicating high statistical precision
found robustness: effect persists across alternative skin tone operationalizations, covariate specifications, and sample definitions
found consistency: unadjusted effect (+0.21pp) is in the same direction as the adjusted effect (+0.43pp), with adjustment increasing the estimate, likely due to confounding by position/league
the analysis was an exploratory, in-sample analysis optimized to maximize supportive evidence

spans.note: caveat that results are an upper bound of in-sample support, not a causal estimate, given unmeasured confounders/specification search/lack of replication
